A lot of people are saying Talos Principle, and it is a really great game, but I want to talk about Antichamber, as not a lot of people seem to be talking about it in here.

Talos Principle is all about systems, you learn a system, you learn how it works, and then they combine those systems together. Antichamber is about subverting those systems with impossibilities which need to be figured out. The best way to describe it is, Talos is a puzzle game, Antichamber is more like one of the older point and click adventure games as far as style and thinking. If you're wanting a puzzle game, Talos is a good game. If you're wanting a game where your thinking is challenged, Antichamber is the way to go.

But, in the end, they are really both worth playing.

If Rachel Dolezal is a Liar, What is Barack Obama?

Choosing to identify more strongly with one of your genuine identities over another is completely different from fabricating an identity.

People of mixed race have to deal with being mis-identified or forced to profess one predominant identity constantly, whether they truly identify with those cultures or not. Once Obama was in the spotlight, he didn't try to erase his family history. Sure, he may have stressed his "blackness" as a campaign strategy, but if he was just another guy walking down the street he would be considered black by the casual observer.

Racial identity is complicated on a personal and social level for those with mixed backgrounds, and to compare these identity decisions to those of this delusional woman is just ignorant.

Racial identity can be complicated. And to be upfront, I argue race is a pretty threadbare definer and something more frequently used to divide. However, I think the column raises some interesting points. Particularly, in the context of people that firmly define as race as a unique identifier. Also, Hughes and Chang raised some good points, points I hadn't considered, about the overall message that Obama's designation on the census could send.

I agree that race as a concept is divisive, and isn't really an indicator of anything aside from social constructs and groupings physical features. However, racial identity is still a more legitimate issue for people who have multiple racial (and therefore cultural) heritages than someone who is appropriating another race and culture, which is why I take issue with the comparison to Dolezal.

In regard to census designation, between the first census that allowed for a mixed race category and the following census, millions of Americans changed their responses. Racial identity for those of mixed race can be fluid, depending on a variety of factors, and a person of mixed race may favor certain of their identities over others on a changing basis. This is partially why I don't think censuses are the most reliable measures of demographics, but any survey of this nature would have similar results. I don't really take issue with Obama's census selection. We, and many others like us, have been guilty of the same.
